candidate_sources.title: Squash (Cucurbita spp.)-Damping-off | Pacific Northwest Pest Management Handbooks
candidate_sources.snippet: Fusarium spp. attack many vegetable seedlings including members of the genus Cucurbita. Infection of the hypocotyl of young plants results in pre- or post-emergence damping-off. Immature seedlings often damp off at the soil line; the hypocotyl and roots turn red-brown. Management includes pasteurized soil mix, drying soil, and seed treatment with Maxim 4FS to control Fusarium and Rhizoctonia spp.

candidate_sources.title: Root Rots (Damping-Off) / Cucurbits / Agriculture: Pest Management Guidelines / UC Statewide IPM Program (UC IPM)
candidate_sources.snippet: Damping-off in cucurbits can be caused by Fusarium spp., Rhizoctonia solani, Pythium spp., and Phytophthora spp. Infection by Fusarium occurs where the seed coat attaches to the hypocotyl; the hypocotyl and roots turn red-brown and the portion above swells slightly. Symptoms include failure to germinate, seedling collapse, and rotted roots near the soil line.

candidate_sources.title: Damping-off in Flower and Vegetable Seedlings | NC State Extension Publications
candidate_sources.snippet: Damping-off may include failure of seeds to germinate, discoloration and rot of young stems near the soil line, and wilting, collapse, and death of young seedlings. Damping-off caused by Fusarium spp. and Rhizoctonia spp. is often a post-emergence damping-off in which the pathogens attack seedlings at the soil line. Management includes pasteurized media and sanitation.

candidate_sources.title: Fusarium Rot of Cucurbits - University of Maine Cooperative Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Fusarium species cause rot of cucurbits including gourds. Fusarium oxysporum has formae speciales specific to various cucurbits, including f. sp. benincasae (wax gourd) and f. sp. lagenariae (calabash gourd). Infection produces red-brown discoloration of the hypocotyl and roots and can cause seedling damping-off.

candidate_sources.title: First Report of Phytophthora Fruit Rot on Bitter Gourd (Momordica charantia) and Sponge Gourd (Luffa cylindrica) Caused by Phytophthora capsici | Plant Health Progress
candidate_sources.snippet: P. capsici has been reported to cause fruit rot on bitter gourd and sponge gourd, with heavy rainfall resulting in rot of >50% of bitter gourd and >25% on sponge gourd in a field in Charleston, SC in September 2014. Fruit rot often occurs on the side of the fruit touching the soil, beginning as a water-soaked lesion covered with white sporulating pathogen growth. Several fungicides effective on watermelon are also labelled for Momordica spp. and edible gourds.

candidate_sources.title: Phytophthora Blight of Cucurbits | Cornell Vegetables
candidate_sources.snippet: Phytophthora blight is caused by the oomycete plant pathogen Phytophthora capsici and can develop on cucurbit plants at any stage of development. Affected crops include cantaloupe, cucumber, gourd, honeydew, pumpkin, squash, and watermelon. The pathogen causes seedling damping-off, leaf spots, foliar blight, root and crown rot, stem lesions, and fruit rot. Fruit lesions become covered in sporangia with a yeast-like, gray to white appearance.

candidate_sources.title: Phytophthora Blight : Vegetable : Center for Agriculture, Food, and the Environment (CAFE) at UMass Amherst
candidate_sources.snippet: Phytophthora blight, caused by Phytophthora capsici, affects cucurbit crops including gourds, pumpkins, and squash. Symptoms include crown rot with water-soaked, collapsed tissue, foliar blight, and fruit rot. The fungus requires very wet conditions for optimal reproduction, and risk greatly increases during periods of heavy rainfall and local flooding events.

candidate_sources.title: Phytophthora blight of cucurbits | APS Education Center
candidate_sources.snippet: Phytophthora blight of cucurbits is caused by Phytophthora capsici. The pathogen infects a wide host range including cucurbits (cucumber, gourd, melon, pumpkin, squash, watermelon) and solanaceous crops, causing damping-off, root and crown rot, foliar blight, and fruit rot.

candidate_sources.title: Powdery mildew of cucurbits | UMN Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Cucurbit powdery mildew causes white, powdery fungal growth on leaves, stems, and petioles. Infection usually begins on older or shaded leaves. Caused by Podosphaera xanthii and Erysiphe cichoracearum. The cucurbit crops most commonly affected are cucumber, gourd, muskmelon, pumpkin, and squash. Time between infection and symptom appearance is usually only 3-7 days.

candidate_sources.title: Cucurbits, Powdery Mildew : Vegetable : Center for Agriculture, Food, and the Environment (CAFE) at UMass Amherst
candidate_sources.snippet: Symptoms occur on both leaf surfaces, stems, and petioles as white, powdery fungal growth, developing first on older and shaded lower leaves. Podosphaera xanthii and Erysiphe cichoracearum are the two most common fungi causing powdery mildew on cucurbits, with P. xanthii being more prevalent and more aggressive. Severe infection can result in early leaf senescence and yield reduction.

candidate_sources.title: Cucurbit Powdery Mildew | Cornell Vegetables
candidate_sources.snippet: Cucurbit powdery mildew fact sheet covering symptoms, the causal pathogens Podosphaera xanthii and Erysiphe (Golovinomyces) cichoracearum, disease cycle, and management including resistant cultivars and fungicide programs for cucumber, melon, squash, pumpkin and gourd.

candidate_sources.title: Cucurbit Powdery Mildew | NC State Extension Publications
candidate_sources.snippet: Cucurbit powdery mildew produces white, powdery fungal growth on leaves, petioles and stems. Caused primarily by Podosphaera xanthii. Favors humid conditions with temperatures around 68-81 F. Affects cucumber, gourd, pumpkin, squash and melon, causing premature leaf death and reduced fruit yield and quality.
